Modelling Antennas with Claude Code

Dorin - ZL4XZ

Introduction

I had always wanted to use antenna modelling software, but never had the time to learn it. Editing the antenna geometry by hand also seemed tedious and discouraging. But with all the recent advances in AI tools, I decided to take a shortcut and let an AI do the hard work. So in about four evenings, an AI assistant took me from an empty folder to a reusable NEC-2 modelling toolkit. Along the way it answered real questions about the 80 m antenna in my garden.

I didn't set out to build a tool. I wanted to know whether I could describe an antenna in plain words, the way I'd describe it to another ham, and get back numbers I could trust. Those numbers were the feed impedance, SWR, gain and take-off angle.

The assistant was Claude Code, a version of Claude that can write and run programs on your own computer. The modelling engine was nec2c, a free version of the classic NEC-2 engine. Claude wrote all the code that joins the two, as I asked questions.

This article follows the work in the order it happened:

  1. A curious first question.
  2. A proof of concept on a 20 m dipole.
  3. A long session on my own 80 m inverted-V fed with ladder line.
  4. Turning the result into antsim, a small toolkit that anyone running Claude Code can use.
  5. Writing this article from those sessions, and checking it against my own experience.

Stage 1: Curiosity

I started with one open-ended prompt in an empty folder:

I want to do a proof of concept for modelling antennas with Claude Code. Let's discuss ways to do that. Starting with a clean directory, and no pre-existing preferences.

Claude didn't start coding. It came back with a few multiple-choice questions, and they were the right ones:

QuestionOptions offeredMy pick
Which antennas first?HF/VHF wire · UHF/microwave/PCB · both, wire firstHF/VHF wire
Which engine?nec2c via deck files · PyNEC/necpp bindings · openEMS (FDTD)nec2c via deck files
What should the PoC show?Describe → results · plots · optimisationDescribe → results, plus plots
First antenna?(several)20 m half-wave dipole

The engine choice mattered most. nec2c was already installed, and its plain-text input files (NEC "decks") also open in xnec2c. That meant I could check anything Claude produced in a program I already trusted. The other options were more powerful, but harder to check.

Stage 2: Proof of concept

The first working version reproduced the textbook dipole. The setup was simple: I describe the wires, and Claude's code writes the NEC input file, runs nec2c, reads the results and draws the plots. Before writing the part that reads the results, Claude ran nec2c once to see its real output rather than guess the format.

20 m half-wave dipoleFree space10 m over average ground
Resonance14.176 MHz14.278 MHz
Impedance at resonance71.7 Ω71.8 Ω
Peak gain2.14 dBi (textbook 2.15)7.10 dBi at 30° elevation

Those numbers matched what I expected, and that is what built my trust. Claude also tuned the length to 10.27 m itself, for the middle of the band in free space, after its first guess resonated about 150 kHz high. At 10 m above ground, the same wire resonated about 100 kHz higher. Finally, it wrote a notes file for itself, CLAUDE.md, so later sessions would know how to use the tool.

The dipole was the simplest case NEC can model. NEC describes an antenna as straight wires, each split into short segments, and calculates the current on every segment. There is no separate feed point: a voltage source is placed on one segment. A dipole is a single straight wire, so the source sits on its middle segment, which is why the wire needs an odd number of segments. That simplicity would hide a problem until the next antenna.

Then I tried something less textbook: a 40 m inverted-V with the apex at 7 m. Unlike the dipole, it is modelled as two wires meeting at the apex, with the source on the segment where they join. Three things in that session set the pattern for the rest of the project:

  • It filled gaps and said so. I hadn't given an included angle. Claude picked 120° because 90° would have put the wire ends almost on the ground, and it told me.
  • Real antennas found real bugs. With more than one wire, NEC numbers the segments across the whole model rather than wire by wire, and Claude's code read the feed-point results wrongly. The single-wire dipole had hidden the problem. Claude found and fixed it in the same session.
  • The tool grew from my questions. I asked for azimuth cuts at 5–60° elevation, then for more distinguishable colours, then whether radiation resistance could be plotted. Each request became a feature.

The radiation-resistance question had the biggest effect. Claude first used nec2c's built-in total of radiated power and noticed that it leaves out the directions straight up and straight down. For a dipole in free space, that showed a 4% loss that doesn't exist. So Claude added up the power over the whole pattern itself, and checked it on the same dipole: 72.3 of 72.4 Ω radiated, 99.8%.

Splitting the input resistance into radiation and loss showed something SWR hides. A low 40 m inverted-V had an SWR of 1.14, but 31.5 of its 56.4 Ω input resistance was ground loss. Its radiation efficiency was 44%.

Stage 3: My 80 m inverted-V on ladder line

The real test was my own antenna: an inverted-V that is a short dipole on 80 m, fed with 450 Ω open-wire line of 10.6 m electrical length. I wanted it resonant on 80 m at the bottom of the feed line, not at the feed point. The model answered with a wire length of about 29 m, pretty close to what I have in real life. It also showed how much the mounting height matters.

The model also held up against the real antenna. With the apex at about 9 m, I measured about 12 Ω at the bottom of the line with a NanoVNA. In the mast-height table below, a 9 m apex falls between the 7 m and 10 m rows, at about 11 Ω. That is within about 1 Ω, and the model's lossless ladder line would be expected to read slightly low.

Short wire, hard match

I wanted to see how shortening a dipole affects how hard it is to match and how efficient it is. I started by running a 20 m-long inverted-V, with the apex 7 m above average ground, on 3.65 MHz as a short dipole. In the model its feed impedance was 11.4 − j998 Ω, with only about 2 Ω of radiation resistance. A low radiation resistance is a warning sign: ground and wire losses then take a bigger share of the power. Lengthening the wire to 30 m gave 27.5 − j418 Ω and three times the radiation resistance.

Claude added its own hand estimates of feedline loss. Through 20 m of RG-213 the 30 m dipole would lose about 7 dB, and through 450 Ω window line about 0.6 dB. (I didn't ask about RG-58, but its loss would surely be much higher.) It was clearly ladder-line territory.

Resonance at the line input

My own antenna is fed with 450 Ω open-wire line, which is also a vital part of the matching, so I asked Claude to include the feeder in the model. Claude added a feeder calculation, checked it against nec2c's own TL card to within 0.1 Ω, and wrote a length solver. The solver tries a range of wire lengths and homes in on each one where the reactance at the shack end is zero.

The feeder is handled outside NEC. nec2c models only the antenna and reports its feed-point impedance at each frequency. Claude's code then works out what that impedance becomes at the bottom of the line, using the standard transmission-line equation. NEC's own TL card does the same job, so it served as the cross-check. Doing it this way had two advantages. One NEC run can be reused for any feeder length, which made the length search and the later multiband search fast. And unlike the TL card, which is lossless, it could later include line loss, a balun and coax.

With the line included, the answer changed completely:

Where it is resonantTotal wireZ at the antennaZ at the shack end
At the line input (towards the shack)28.91 m25.4 − j473 Ω12.0 + j0 Ω
At the antenna feed point39.07 m51.2 − j0.1 Ω106 + j461 Ω

I only cared about resonances at the line input with a fairly low impedance, below 500 Ω. Claude added that as a filter and scanned wire lengths from 12 to 150 m. It found exactly two: 28.91 m at 12 Ω, and 109.6 m at 49.5 Ω. The 110 m wire gives a near-perfect 50 Ω match but radiates only 9% of the power, because it is a long, low wire just above the soil. Claude saved my preference, so later sessions skip that solution without being told.

How mast height affects efficiency

Next I compared the masts I could actually put up. The resonant length barely moved, because the feeder sets most of the reactance. The efficiency changed a lot.

Apex / endsResonant wireZ at shackRadiation efficiencyGain at 30°
7 m / 2 m28.91 m12.1 Ω22%−4.2 dBi
10 m / 2 m29.14 m10.7 Ω31%−2.6 dBi
12 m / 2 m29.37 m9.2 Ω36%−1.9 dBi
12 m / 4 m29.39 m10.2 Ω44%−0.6 dBi

Modelled results on 3.65 MHz for the mast heights I could put up, over average ground. For each one, the wire length was tuned for resonance at the bottom of the 450 Ω line, and "Z at shack" is the resistance there, which a 1:4 transformer can easily match to 50 Ω.

On 40 m, the same 29.14 m wire through the same feeder came out at 60.4 − j193.9 Ω at the shack on 7.1 MHz. That needs a tuner, but radiation efficiency was 54%, and it beat a dedicated resonant 40 m inverted-V dipole at 7 m at every elevation angle, by 0.6 to 1.8 dB.

All these results came from plain-English questions I typed into the chat sessions. In my excitement, I was experimenting freely rather than working systematically.

Multiband, the G5RV and the ZS6BKW

Then I asked the big question. With 7–11 m of 450 Ω line and 10 m of coax, which lengths keep SWR below 3:1 on ten bands, 80 m to 6 m? Claude wrote a multiband search and tried 34,773 combinations. Because it reused the same NEC results for every feeder combination, the search was quick.

The answer: none. The best combination reached 3 of 10 bands. A fixed wire plus a fixed matching section only lines up with 50 Ω on a few bands.

I asked, half joking, whether the G5RV and its variants are a scam. Claude said "scam" is too strong: the antenna is legitimate but oversold. Louis Varney designed it for 20 m and said other bands need a tuner. The model agreed, with 20 m closest and SWR 50–80 on 60, 30, 17 and 10 m.

The ZS6BKW reached SWR below 3 across the whole of 40, 20, 17 and 12 m, which matches what is published about it. Claude pointed out that the matching section has to be about 13.3 m electrical, roughly 12 m of physical window line.

Matching networks

In a later session I asked for matching networks at the bottom of the line. Claude worked through per-band L-networks, then a link-coupled tuner, then a T200-2 toroid version, and finally a single simple configuration for all bands.

Stage 4: From experiment to toolkit

One prompt turned the experiment into a reusable tool: "transform this project into a more general purpose harness to enable antenna modelling using claude code." The result is antsim, a small toolkit with eight ready-made example antennas, from a 20 m dipole to a 3-element Yagi. It handles wire loss, traps and loading coils, and feeders made of ladder line, a balun and coax. It also warns about common modelling mistakes and has a quick self-test.

The most important part isn't the code but CLAUDE.md, a plain-English instruction sheet for Claude. It holds the workflow (describe, model, run, check, tune, report) and the NEC-2 rules of thumb I'd otherwise repeat in every session.

Stage 5: Writing this article

This article was written with Claude's help too. I asked it to go back through my Claude Code sessions and draft the story of the project, in the order things happened. The numbers in it come from those sessions.

Then I reviewed the draft paragraph by paragraph, to check that it made sense and reflected what I actually experienced. I left comments in the doc, and Claude answered them or made the changes. Some things only I could add, such as my NanoVNA measurement and details of my real antenna. Claude also proofread my additions and cut back the software details, since most readers are radio amateurs rather than programmers.

What worked and what to watch

The AI was most useful as a fast, tireless modelling partner that writes its own tools. It was least useful when I accepted a number without a cross-check.

What worked

  • Questions became features. I never designed the tool. Each question I asked about my antenna left a capability behind: azimuth cuts, efficiency, feedlines, the solver, the multiband search.
  • Checks against known answers. A 73 Ω dipole, 100% efficiency in free space, the TL card within 0.1 Ω, published ZS6BKW behaviour. Each new feature was checked against something I could easily fact-check.
  • Stated assumptions. When I left something out, such as the included angle, ground, wire gauge or band edges, it chose a value and told me. I could correct it in one line.
  • Explanations, not just numbers. "SWR 1.14 hides 56% ground loss" taught me more than a table would have.
  • Speed. A 5° pattern over real ground runs in seconds, and the multiband results can be re-sorted in seconds. I tried mast heights I would never have bothered to model by hand.

What to watch

  • The AI can be wrong, and confident. It made a sign error in capacitor loss and overwrote an output folder. It caught and reported both by itself, but only because the workflow asks it to check.
  • Hand estimates are not simulation. Several loss figures (coax, tuner, ladder line) came from formulas rather than NEC. Claude labelled them that way, and that labelling matters.
  • NEC-2 has limits. It can't model buried or ground-touching wires, and lossless lines hide real loss. The model is a good guide, not a measurement.
  • Look at the plots. Open swr.png and the pattern plots yourself, and the 3D view in xnec2c. A plausible-looking summary is not the same as a correct model.

Try it yourself

You don't need to know NEC-2's card format to start. You do need to know enough about antennas to tell when an answer is wrong.

antsim is on GitHub at github.com/dcustura/antsim. To try it you need a Linux computer (or Windows with WSL) with nec2c, Python 3.10 or newer, and the numpy and matplotlib packages, plus Claude Code.

Run Claude Code in the antsim folder and ask, in plain English, how to use it and whether everything it needs is installed. If something is missing, Claude will offer to install it or show you how.

After that, describe your antenna to Claude the way you'd describe it on the air: "a 40 m inverted-V, apex 12 m, ends 3 m, fed with 20 m of RG-58, tune it for 7.1 MHz". It writes the model, runs it, checks it, and reports resonance, SWR bandwidth, gain, take-off angle and efficiency.

What began as "let's discuss ways to do that" ended with a better understanding of my own antenna. A wire of about 29 m is right for my feeder. The ends matter as much as the apex. And no length of wire and ladder line will make a tuner unnecessary on ten bands.
